title: Chapter 4 Mastery Quiz: Observational, Descriptive & Qualitative Methods
description: Master naturalistic and structured observation, observer bias, participant reactivity, single-case studies, and thematic analysis.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of naturalistic observation over laboratory experiments?

options.text: High experimental control over confounding variables
High ecological validity, capturing spontaneous real-world behavior
The ability to firmly establish cause-and-effect relationships
Zero requirement for ethical review

questions.explanation: Naturalistic observation observes behavior in genuine real-life settings, giving it exceptional ecological validity.

questions.question: What is Mary Ainsworth's famous 'Strange Situation' protocol an example of?

options.text: Structured (laboratory) observation
Naturalistic observation in a forest
Archival census analysis
Double-blind pharmacological trial

questions.explanation: The Strange Situation uses a standardized laboratory sequence of episodes to observe infant attachment behaviors under controlled conditions.

questions.question: In participant observation, what is the major risk known as 'going native'?

options.text: Forgetting to record participant demographic data
Becoming so emotionally and culturally identified with the group that scientific objectivity is lost
Contracting a tropical illness while conducting field research
Refusing to accept research grant funding

questions.explanation: 'Going native' occurs when a participant observer over-identifies with the observed group, losing neutral analytical perspective.

questions.question: What is participant reactivity?

options.text: An allergic reaction to laboratory stimuli
A change in behavior that occurs because the participant is aware of being observed
The statistical power of an interaction term in ANOVA
The delay between stimulus presentation and verbal recall

questions.explanation: Reactivity (such as the Hawthorne Effect) happens when people modify their actions because they know someone is watching them.

questions.question: Which methodological technique is designed to eliminate participant reactivity by allowing participants to become accustomed to the presence of an observer over time?

options.text: Habituation
Counterbalancing
Double-blinding
Stratified random sampling

questions.explanation: Habituation involves extended exposure to observers until participants view them as background furniture and return to natural behavior.

questions.question: An observer records the frequency of aggressive behaviors during a school recess. If the observer expects boys to be more aggressive than girls, their tendency to interpret ambiguous shoves as aggression exclusively in boys is an example of:

options.text: Observer Bias (Expectancy Bias)
The Hawthorne Effect
Attrition
Regression to the mean

questions.explanation: Observer bias occurs when an observer's personal expectations or hypotheses influence how they perceive and record behaviors.

questions.question: What is the most effective methodological remedy to protect against observer bias in behavioral coding?

options.text: Using observers who are blind to the study hypotheses and group conditions
Paying observers double their hourly rate
Instructing observers to use intuitive gut feelings
Removing operational definitions from the codebook

questions.explanation: Using blind raters who do not know the hypotheses or participant conditions prevents expectations from biasing coding.

questions.question: Measuring which book sections in a public library have the most worn and torn carpet is an example of:

options.text: A physical trace (unobtrusive) measure
A semi-structured qualitative interview
A within-subjects experimental design
A Latin square counterbalancing technique

questions.explanation: Physical trace measures evaluate behavioral erosion or accretion without interacting with or disrupting participants.

questions.question: In behavioral observation, what does 'Time Sampling' involve?

options.text: Recording behaviors during pre-specified, structured time intervals (e.g., 10 seconds every 2 minutes)
Waiting for a behavioral event to occur and recording its total clock duration
Asking participants to guess what time it is
Conducting studies exclusively between 9:00 AM and 5:00 PM

questions.explanation: Time sampling involves dividing the observation period into intervals and recording whether target behaviors occur during each interval.

questions.question: What is the primary scientific limitation of the single-case study method (e.g., Patient H.M. or Phineas Gage)?

options.text: It cannot generate novel hypotheses
It lacks generalizability and cannot establish causal laws for the broader population
It requires expensive neuroimaging in every instance
It is banned by the American Psychological Association

questions.explanation: Because a single individual (N = 1) may possess idiosyncratic traits or unique brain variations, findings cannot be widely generalized.

questions.question: How did the case of Phineas Gage advance psychological science?

options.text: It proved that vision is processed in the occipital lobe
It provided early clinical evidence linking the prefrontal cortex to personality, social inhibition, and emotional control
It established the need for double-blind survey methods
It demonstrated that operant conditioning cures brain damage

questions.explanation: Gage's dramatic personality changes following severe bilateral ventromedial prefrontal cortex damage localized social-emotional regulation to frontal lobes.

questions.question: A researcher evaluates whether temperature correlates with violent crime by examining 20 years of city police arrest logs. What research design is this?

options.text: Archival research
Participant observation
Laboratory experiment
Qualitative thematic focus group

questions.explanation: Analyzing pre-existing organizational or government records collected for non-research purposes is archival research.

questions.question: What is a major limitation of archival research?

options.text: Extreme participant reactivity during data collection
The researcher has no control over which variables were recorded or how accurately they were measured by original record-keepers
It is impossible to analyze longitudinal trends
It is always classified as Full Board review by IRBs

questions.explanation: Because archival records were compiled by third parties, important variables may be missing, inconsistent, or categorized inadequately.

questions.question: What distinguishes qualitative research from quantitative research?

options.text: Qualitative research focuses on narrative meaning and lived experience rather than numerical statistical tests
Qualitative research never collects data from humans
Qualitative research is only conducted by medical doctors
Quantitative research does not care about accuracy

questions.explanation: Qualitative research analyzes narrative, linguistic, and visual data to explore subjective meanings and complex contexts.

questions.question: What is a semi-structured interview?

options.text: An interview with rigid yes/no questions where the interviewer cannot deviate from a script
An interview guided by open-ended questions and flexible prompts that allow the interviewer to explore emergent topics
An interview conducted by a computer algorithm without human presence
A casual chat in a hallway without any planned questions

questions.explanation: Semi-structured interviews use a prepared guide with open-ended flexibility to follow up on unexpected participant insights.

questions.question: In thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006), what is the first fundamental step?

options.text: Calculating statistical correlations in SPSS
Familiarizing oneself with the data through repeated, active reading of transcripts
Publishing the results in an academic journal
Deleting half the transcripts to save time

questions.explanation: Phase 1 requires deep immersion and familiarization with the textual data by reading and re-reading transcripts.

questions.question: What is a 'code' in qualitative analysis?

options.text: A computer password used to encrypt audio recordings
A concise label identifying an interesting or meaningful feature of the textual data
A secret chemical formula used in neuroimaging
The p-value associated with a chi-square test

questions.explanation: In qualitative coding, a code is a descriptive or conceptual tag assigned to a segment of text to capture its core meaning.

questions.question: How does a 'theme' differ from a 'code' in thematic analysis?

options.text: Themes are broad patterns of shared meaning across multiple codes; codes are specific granular text tags
Codes are used only in psychology; themes are used only in literature
Themes are generated by computers, while codes are written by humans
There is no difference; they are exact synonyms

questions.explanation: Themes represent broader organizing concepts that capture unified patterns of meaning across multiple clustered codes.

questions.question: What is 'reflexivity' in qualitative research?

options.text: The knee-jerk patellar response tested by doctors
The critical self-awareness and transparent examination of how the researcher's own identity and biases influence the research process
The speed of typing interview transcripts
The requirement to only study reflexive motor movements

questions.explanation: Reflexivity requires researchers to critically examine their personal beliefs, social position, and assumptions to acknowledge how they shape interpretations.

questions.question: What is the typical ideal size of a focus group in psychological research?

options.text: 1 to 2 people
6 to 10 people
50 to 100 people
1,000 people in a stadium

questions.explanation: A group of 6 to 10 participants allows rich dynamic interaction while ensuring every member has adequate opportunity to speak.

questions.question: What is 'triangulation' in descriptive and qualitative methodologies?

options.text: Using three separate statistical tests on a single variable
Synthesizing multiple data sources, methods, or observers to cross-verify findings
Interviewing three siblings from the same family
Restricting study time to 3:00 PM every day

questions.explanation: Methodological triangulation uses diverse data streams (e.g., observation, interviews, surveys) to build robust, corroborated conclusions.

questions.question: An observational study of maternal-infant bonding produces an inter-rater reliability of Cohen's Kappa = 0.89. What does this indicate?

options.text: Very poor agreement between raters
Strong, robust agreement between independent observers, demonstrating a reliable coding system
The null hypothesis must be accepted
The study suffered from severe participant attrition

questions.explanation: A Cohen's Kappa above 0.80 represents strong to near-perfect inter-rater agreement beyond chance, confirming coding reliability.
